raw_case_text:
A 78-year-old woman was diagnosed 4 months before admission with a right frontal GBM with extension to the basal ganglia and temporal lobe. The patient underwent a frontal craniotomy and partial resection of the lesion, followed by hypofractionated radiation therapy (16 fractions of 250 cGy) with concomitant daily TMZ (75 mg/m2). During the concurrent phase, she developed grade 1 lymphopenia and grade 2 nausea, but the treatment was otherwise well tolerated. Two days after completing chemoradiation, the patient was admitted for dyspnea and asymmetrical lower extremity edema. At admission, she denied cough, sputum, hemoptysis or thoracic pain. She reported no fever, chills, sweats or weight loss. Neurologic symptoms were stable since her last assessment. She had a history of hypertension and controlled type 2 diabetes. Medications included omeprazole, amlodipine, metformin, gliclazide, sitagliptin and prophylactic sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim. She was also taking dexamethasone 4 mg/day on a tapering scale.
Upon physical examination, she had normal vital signs, with a respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min and oxygen saturation of 95% on room air. She had asymmetric edema of the lower limbs and, on auscultation, fine respiratory crackles bilaterally. Electrolytes, liver enzymes and renal function were normal. Blood counts were: hemoglobin 11.9 g/dl, platelets 67,000/mm3 and leukocytes 7,030/mm3, with an absolute lymphocyte count of 800/mm3. A venous duplex-scan of the lower extremities showed an extensive deep vein thrombosis involving the left common femoral vein. An angiotomography of the thorax diagnosed an acute pulmonary embolism and also revealed scattered lobulated nodules with areas of cavitation, measuring up to 2.7 cm, located predominately in the upper lobes, some with a surrounding ground-glass halo. There was no pleural effusion. Areas of peribronchial infiltrates and centrilobular nodules were also present (fig. 1). Serum galactomannan levels, determined using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, were elevated (optical density index = 6.7, optical density index >=0.5 is considered a positive result). Blood samples obtained for culture and Cryptococcus neoformans and Histoplasma antigen assays were negative.
A CT-guided pulmonary biopsy was then performed. Histochemical analysis (Gomori's silver stain) showed septate hyphal elements with acute-angle branching (fig. 2), and culture of the pulmonary tissue was positive for Aspergillus fumigatus. The patient was promptly started on antifungal therapy with voriconazole and was discharged to complete the treatment as an outpatient. Chemotherapy with TMZ was resumed after 4 weeks of antifungal therapy. A control CT scan done approximately 30 days after admission revealed a reduction of the nodular lesions and ground-glass component previously identified (fig. 3).
Written informed consent for publication of the clinical details and/or clinical images was obtained from the guardian/relative of the patient.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 78-year-old woman with glioblastoma multiforme presented 2 days after completing concurrent chemoradiation with acute dyspnea and asymmetrical lower extremity edema.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Four months prior to admission, the patient underwent partial resection of a right frontal glioblastoma multiforme followed by hypofractionated radiotherapy (16 fractions of 250 cGy) with concurrent daily temozolomide (75 mg/m2) and tapering dexamethasone (4 mg/day), complicated by grade 1 lymphopenia. Two days after completing chemoradiation, she presented with acute dyspnea and asymmetrical left lower limb swelling without fever or cough.
subjective.past_medical_history: Right frontal glioblastoma multiforme (extending to the basal ganglia and temporal lobe) diagnosed 4 months prior, status post partial craniotomy resection and concurrent temozolomide/radiotherapy; hypertension; controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for acute dyspnea and asymmetrical lower limb edema; negative for cough, sputum, hemoptysis, chest pain, fever, chills, night sweats, weight loss, or neurological deterioration. Home medications: dexamethasone 4 mg/day, TMP-SMX prophylaxis, omeprazole, amlodipine, metformin, gliclazide, and sitagliptin.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs were normal with respiratory rate 18 breaths/min and room-air SpO2 95%. Physical exam showed asymmetrical lower extremity edema (left > right), bilateral fine inspiratory crackles on lung auscultation, and stable neurological exam.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, thrombocytopenia (platelets 67,000/mm3), WBC 7,030/mm3 with lymphopenia (absolute lymphocyte count 800/mm3), and normal electrolytes, liver enzymes, and renal function. Blood cultures and serum Cryptococcus neoformans and Histoplasma antigen assays were negative. Lower extremity venous duplex ultrasound confirmed extensive deep vein thrombosis of the left common femoral vein.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic CT angiography confirmed an acute pulmonary embolism and simultaneously revealed scattered lobulated, cavitary pulmonary nodules up to 2.7 cm predominantly in the upper lobes—some with a surrounding ground-glass halo sign—along with peribronchial infiltrates and centrilobular nodules without pleural effusion. Serum galactomannan ELISA was strongly positive (optical density index 6.7; cutoff >=0.5). CT-guided lung biopsy histopathology (Gomori methenamine silver stain) demonstrated septate hyphae with acute-angle branching, and lung tissue culture grew Aspergillus fumigatus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Proven cavitary invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (Aspergillus fumigatus) coexisting with left common femoral deep vein thrombosis and acute pulmonary embolism in a patient with glioblastoma multiforme following concurrent temozolomide chemoradiation and dexamethasone therapy, confirmed by positive serum galactomannan (ODI 6.7), CT halo and cavitary nodules, and CT-guided lung biopsy GMS histopathology and culture. Treated with oral voriconazole, achieving marked reduction of pulmonary nodules and ground-glass halos on 30-day follow-up chest CT and enabling safe resumption of adjuvant temozolomide chemotherapy after 4 weeks of antifungal therapy.
